fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Grammar Quiz
fields.features_subheading: Describe who takes the quiz and what a score triggers. Emergent builds the questions, the bands, and the table answers land in.
fields.feature_1:
Questions drafted for the rules you pick

Name the rules to cover, such as comma splices or subject-verb agreement, and Emergent drafts a question for each in a real sentence. A follow-up prompt rewrites any you dislike.
fields.feature_2:
The rule shown after every answer

Each question can show a short explanation once answered, so a miss teaches the rule instead of just costing a point. You write the explanation or edit the drafted one by prompt.
fields.feature_3:
Score bands that place, pass, or decline

Set bands once, such as 0 to 6 for Foundations, and the app assigns each taker a result the moment they finish. A pass mark can send an email with no one reviewing scores.
fields.feature_4:
Every answer lands in a table you own

Each submission saves as a row with the taker, the question, and the rule it tests. Sort the table by rule, and the one your takers keep missing sits at the top of the list.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen, no response caps

Takers answer one question per screen on a phone, and Emergent puts no cap on how many people answer. A quiz on your site can take 40 responses in a term or 4,000 in a week.
fields.feature_6:
Your own domain, and code you can keep

A custom domain is included in Emergent and uses credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and rerun the same quiz next term with a new question set.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Grammar Quizzes, Four Different Jobs
fields.tab_content_1:
A 15-question quiz sorts enrollment into 3 levels

Tidemark Language School enrolls 40 new students each term, and each one takes a 15-question grammar quiz at sign-up. Score bands set the 3 levels, and 0 to 6 lands in Foundations. This term the quiz placed 9 students in Foundations, 22 in Intermediate, and 9 in Advanced before the first class met.
fields.tab_content_2:
The decline goes out with no editor reading tests

Quillstone Content sends each freelance applicant a 10-question grammar quiz with a pass mark of 8. Anyone under the mark gets a decline email the same day; anyone at or over it gets a paid test piece. Of the last 31 applicants, 12 passed and 19 got declines, and only passing names reached the editors' Slack channel.
fields.tab_content_3:
One missed rule, 3 straight Fridays, a Tuesday group

Every Friday, the 26 ninth graders in Rowanfield High's English class take a 5-question grammar quiz on the week's rules. The results table tracks misses by rule and student. When one rule, comma splices, showed the same 6 students missing it on 3 straight Fridays, their teacher booked a Tuesday small group.
fields.tab_content_4:
The quiz emails each taker the rule they missed most

Marisol Vega sells an online punctuation course, and a free grammar quiz on her site is how readers find it. When a taker finishes, the app emails them a short lesson on the rule they missed most and saves their score. Last month, 180 people took the quiz and 42 of them started the course.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Grammar Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a grammar quiz whose wrong answers are real mistakes and whose score tells you what to teach next.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the rules the quiz covers
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Decide what a score should trigger
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write each question as a real sentence
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick 5 to 8 rules you see in real writing, such as comma splices, apostrophes, and subject-verb agreement. A quiz built on the mistakes your takers actually make reads as fair, and the results tell you something you can act on.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Decide what happens at each band before you write a question: a placement level, a pass mark with a decline email, or a lesson sent to the taker. The trigger shapes how many questions you need and how hard they should be.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write each question as a sentence someone could have typed, then ask what fixes it or which version is correct. A rule quoted from a handbook tests memory; a sentence with the error in place tests the skill you care about.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give every question 3 or 4 options, and make each wrong one a mistake people actually type, such as its for it's. An option nobody would pick pads the question without telling you anything about the taker.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Explain the miss, not just the score
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write one or two lines per question that name the rule and show the corrected sentence. A taker who sees why their pick failed leaves knowing more than they arrived with, and a screening quiz can skip this screen entirely.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Build it and take it yourself
fields.howto_step_6_des: Describe the quiz, the bands, and the trigger in one prompt, and Emergent builds the questions, the scoring, and the table behind them. Take it yourself before anyone else does, and fix any question you can argue two answers for.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Watch the results and swap questions
fields.howto_step_7_des: Sort the results by question once real answers arrive. A question everyone gets right is not pulling its weight, and one everyone misses may be badly worded rather than hard; rewrite either with a follow-up prompt and keep the score bands as they are.

faq_plan.a: A grammar quiz is a short test of whether someone can spot and fix errors in written sentences: punctuation, agreement, verb forms, and commonly confused words. Each question shows a sentence and asks which version is correct or what fixes it, and the score shows which rules the taker knows and which need work.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a grammar quiz?
faq_plan.a: Start with 5 to 8 rules your takers actually get wrong, write one sentence-based question per rule, and choose what each score band leads to. With Emergent's AI survey builder, you describe the quiz in a prompt and get working questions, score bands, and a results table saved to a database you own.

faq_plan.q: What is the difference between an English quiz and a grammar quiz?
faq_plan.a: An English quiz can cover anything in the subject: literature, vocabulary, spelling, comprehension, or grammar. A grammar quiz tests one slice, the rules for building correct sentences. If you are placing students or screening writers, the narrower quiz gives a cleaner signal, because every miss maps to a rule you can teach or flag.

faq_plan.q: Can I build a free grammar quiz for my website?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing. A free grammar quiz on a course site or class page is a sensible first build, and the same approach runs a geography quiz when you need one.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a grammar quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Match the length to the job: 10 to 15 questions place students reliably, 8 to 10 screen applicants, and 5 work for a weekly class check. Write 1 or 2 grammar quiz questions per rule you care about and stop there. A taker should finish in one sitting.

faq_plan.q: Should a grammar quiz show the answers at the end?
faq_plan.a: Show them when the quiz teaches, and hide them when it screens. A class or placement quiz that reviews the grammar quiz questions and answers together at the end turns each miss into a lesson. A screening quiz keeps them hidden, since the score is the point.

faq_plan.q: Can a grammar quiz place students into class levels?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Set score bands when you build it, with the lowest band feeding your foundations group, and each taker lands in a level the moment they finish. When the placement matters, pair it with a vocabulary quiz. One bad day on one test should not set a student's level alone.

faq_plan.q: Can I use a grammar quiz to screen freelance writers?
faq_plan.a: Yes, as a first gate. Set a pass mark, let the quiz send the decline or the next step on its own, and keep a short paid test piece for whoever clears it. The app emails each applicant their result, and editors see only the names that passed.

faq_plan.q: How do I see which rules students miss most on a grammar quiz?
faq_plan.a: Save every answer with the rule it tests, then sort or filter by rule. In an app built with Emergent, each response is a row in a table you own. One filter shows the rule a class keeps missing, by week or by student, with no copying into a spreadsheet.

faq_plan.q: Can I reuse my grammar quiz app for another subject?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The questions, options, and explanations are content; the scoring, bands, and results table are the app. A prompt swaps the question set, and the build that runs your grammar quiz can run a bible quiz for a youth group next term.

quiz.title: Grammar Quiz: 8 Sentences, How Many Can You Fix?
quiz.intro: Eight sentences with the errors people actually type. Pick one answer per question; your score and the rule behind each answer show at the end.

questions.text: Which sentence uses its or it's correctly?

options.text: The team lost it's last game.
The team lost its last game.
The team lost its' last game.
The team lost their's last game.

questions.explanation: Its is a possessive pronoun, like hers or theirs, and possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

source.quote: The personal pronouns hers, ours, yours, theirs, its, whose, and the pronoun oneself never take an apostrophe.

questions.text: The lounge belongs to all the teachers. Which phrase is correct?
questions.explanation: Teachers is a plural ending in s, so the apostrophe goes after the s to show that the lounge belongs to all of them.

source.quote: To show plural possession, simply put an apostrophe after the s.

questions.text: Which version fixes this comma splice: I finished the report, I sent it to Dana.

options.text: I finished the report I sent it to Dana.
I finished the report, I then sent it to Dana.
I finished the report. I sent it to Dana.
I finished, the report, I sent it to Dana.

questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone make a comma splice. Ending the first clause with a period fixes it.

source.quote: run two independent clauses together by using a comma instead of a period

questions.text: Neither the coach nor the players ___ happy with the schedule.
questions.explanation: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Players is plural, so the verb is are.

source.quote: The verb in an or, either/or, or neither/nor sentence agrees with the noun or pronoun closest to it.

questions.text: The new schedule will ___ every shift on the weekend.
questions.explanation: The blank needs a verb, an action done to every shift. Affect is the verb; effect is the noun for the outcome.

source.quote: affect is typically used as a verb that refers to an action

questions.text: Which sign is correct for a checkout lane?
questions.explanation: Items can be counted one by one, and countable things take fewer.

source.quote: Fewer refers to things that are countable.

questions.text: Every afternoon, the dog ___ in the sun by the window.
questions.explanation: The dog is resting, not putting something down, so the verb is lie, and in the present tense it is lies.

source.quote: To lie is to rest or recline

questions.text: Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?

options.text: Whom called the office this morning?
Who called the office this morning?
Whom did called the office this morning?
Who's called the office this morning?

questions.explanation: The blank is the subject of called. Swap in he or she: she called, so the subject form who is right.

source.quote: Use who wherever you would use the subjective pronouns I, he, she, we, or they.
